extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism researchers, and readers interested in media studies and survey methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and critiquing survey research that claims to measure public support for core journalism values — including question design, scoring rules, reporting, and comparative sampling. Useful for journalists, researchers, and editors deciding how to present such findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: “This value measures how strongly a person feels there is a need to monitor people in power and know what public officials are doing or saying. The flip side of this value is worry about intrusiveness or this oversight becoming a hindrance, getting in the way, or placing too much importance on insignificant events.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with four statements (agree with 1 and 3, disagree with 2 and 4 indicate support): 1) The powerful need to be monitored or they will be inclined to abuse their power. 2) It’s important to put some trust in authority figures so they can do their jobs. 3) It’s vital that the public know what government leaders are doing and saying each day. 4) Leaders need to be able to do some things behind closed doors to fulfill their duties. (Example results reported: 70% agree / 8% disagree with statement 1; 66% agree / 12% disagree with statement 3; 50% agree / 27% disagree with statement 4.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is the idea that transparency is usually the best cure for what’s wrong in the world, and that on balance it’s usually better for things to be public than for things to be kept secret. The inverse is that sometimes the need to keep things secret is more important than the public’s right to know and that most problems can be solved without embarrassing facts being laid out in the open.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with four statements (agree with 1 and 3, disagree with 2 and 4 indicate support): 1) On balance, it’s usually better for the public to know than for things to be kept secret. 2) Sometimes the need to keep a secret outweighs the public’s right to know. 3) Transparency is usually the best cure for what’s wrong in the world. 4) Most problems can be addressed without putting embarrassing facts in the open. (Example results reported: e.g., 69% agree / 9% disagree with statement 1.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Factualism
rubrics_metrics.description: “This value measures whether on balance more facts are always better and facts are the key to knowing what is true. The flip side is that the truth is more than just a matter of adding facts and that this emphasis on factualism can mask bias.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with four statements (agree with 1 and 3, disagree with 2 and 4 indicate support): 1) The more facts people have, the more likely it is they will get to the truth. 2) A lot of the time you know enough about something and more facts don't help. 3) For most things, knowing what’s true is a matter of gathering evidence and proof. 4) For a lot of things that matter, facts only get you so far. (Example results reported: 71% agree / 7% disagree with statement 1; statement 2 was the only one with more disagreement than agreement: 31% agree / 48% disagree.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving voice to the less powerful
rubrics_metrics.description: “This value measures whether people want to amplify the voices of people who aren’t ordinarily heard and if a society should be judged on how it treats the least fortunate. The inverse instinct is that inequalities will always exist and favoring the least fortunate does not always help them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with four statements (agree with 1 and 3, disagree with 2 and 4 indicate support): 1) A society should be judged by how it treats its least fortunate. 2) Sometimes favoring the least fortunate doesn’t actually help them. 3) It’s important to offer a voice to the voiceless. 4) Inequalities will always exist and you can’t eliminate them. (Example results: 74% agree / 4% disagree with statement 3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Social criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: “This value measures how important people think it is to put a spotlight on a community’s problems in order to solve them. The flip side puts more emphasis on the value of celebrating things that are going right or working well in order to reinforce them and encourage more of them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with four statements (agree with 1 and 3, disagree with 2 and 4 indicate support): 1) We need to put a spotlight on problems in society in order to solve them. 2) Too much focus on what’s wrong can make things worse. 3) The way to make a society stronger is through criticizing what’s wrong. 4) The way to make a society stronger is through celebrating what’s right. (Example results: 72% agree / 6% disagree with statement 1; 43% agree / 35% disagree with statement 3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'supporter' (stringent composite standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study counts someone as a 'supporter' of a journalism value only if they 'on average at least slightly agree with the two affirmative statements and slightly disagree with the two contradictory statements' used to measure each value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arbitrary, conjunctive rule (must both agree with positives AND disagree with negatives) substantially lowers measured support compared with reporting single-statement agreement rates; it can produce results like labeling ~30% as supporters for values where single-item agreement was 60–70%. Reporters and researchers should be explicit about this cutoff and not conflate the composite standard with simple endorsement. The author shows that many respondents agreed with both affirmative and 'negative' items, meaning the composite rule misclassifies nuanced views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question framing balance / avoid asymmetric phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The affirmative statements (intended to indicate support) are general civic principles, while the negative statements tend to be limited-exception phrased — making it easy for respondents to agree with both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design balanced item wording so 'affirmative' and 'negative' items are comparable in tone and scope; avoid treating reasonable, nuanced exceptions as the 'antithesis' of a principle. The page argues that framing negatives as sensible qualifications (e.g., 'sometimes secrets are necessary') will lead many respondents to agree with both sides, so researchers should anticipate and address that in measurement and scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include journalists in comparative measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The study measures thousands of civilians but does not survey journalists, yet frames findings as implying a gap between journalists and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the research claims journalists and the public differ on values, it should include a representative sample of journalists (or reference existing data on journalists' views). Without measuring journalists, conclusions about a journalist-public gap are unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalized reporting; accurately represent methodological nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticizes headlines and coverage that translate the study’s composite measures into claims like 'the public doesn’t share our values,' calling this 'mistrust porn' and a distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and editors should avoid binary, sensational headlines that ignore methodological definitions (e.g., composite cutoffs), and should present the nuance — including single-item agreement rates, scoring rules, and uncertainty — to prevent exaggerating distance between journalists and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster analysis is useful but label carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The study clusters respondents into groups (The Upholders, The Moralists, The Journalism Supporters, and The Indifferent) and uses those clusters in analysis and experimental manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluster analysis can be informative for slicing attitudes, but cluster names should not imply normative judgments (e.g., labeling 20% 'The Journalism Supporters' misleadingly suggests the other 80% don't support journalism). Researchers and reporters should choose neutral labels and explain what clusters actually represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting survey items and response distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the actual survey statements and the agree/disagree splits so readers can judge item wording and apparent contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists all 20 statements and their agree/disagree percentages as an example of good transparency; publishing full items and distributions enables readers to evaluate framing effects and the plausibility of composite scoring rules.
